patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral leg weakness, foot drop, and hand clumsiness over 14 months — difficulty walking upstairs and rising from chairs
patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old software engineer presented to neurology clinic with a 14-month history of progressive bilateral lower and upper extremity weakness and sensory loss. He initially noticed difficulty rising from low chairs approximately 14 months ago, which he attributed to being sedentary at his desk job. Over the following months he developed progressive bilateral foot drop — he began tripping on stairs and uneven pavement. He now cannot walk up stairs without pulling himself up by the railing with both arms. Approximately 8 months ago he began noticing hand weakness and clumsiness — he drops objects, has difficulty typing, and struggled to open jars. His wife first noticed his hands looked thinner in the web spaces. He has also had diffuse paresthesias in a glove-and-stocking distribution — not particularly painful, but a persistent uncomfortable tingling. He saw his internist who found depressed reflexes and referred him to neurology. He has no prior history of diabetes, alcohol use, toxic exposures, family history of neuropathy, or recent infections. He has never been treated for neuropathy. The progression over 14 months is subacute-chronic, affecting both proximal and distal muscles and both sensory and motor functions — a pattern atypical for diabetic or hereditary neuropathy and concerning for an acquired demyelinating polyneuropathy.

neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral proximal weakness — hip flexors 3+/5, hip abductors 4/5. Distal: ankle dorsiflexion 3/5 bilateral, EHL 3/5. Bilateral wrist extension 4/5, bilateral hand intrinsics 4/5, APB 3+/5. Mild atrophy bilateral thenar and hypothenar muscles.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral stocking-and-glove sensory loss — reduced light touch, pinprick, and vibration bilaterally to knees (lower) and wrists (upper). Proprioception mildly reduced at bilateral great toes.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Ankle reflexes absent bilaterally. Knee jerks absent bilaterally. Biceps 1+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis absent bilaterally. Triceps absent bilaterally. Plantar flexors bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Heel-shin mildly ataxic. Finger-nose mildly clumsy (weakness).
neurological_exam.gait: Bilateral steppage gait — bilateral foot drop. Trendelenburg gait component (hip girdle weakness). Moderate difficulty rising from chair. Cannot run. TUG 18 seconds.
neurological_exam.additional: Mild thenar and hypothenar atrophy bilaterally. No pes cavus. No hammer toes. No Mees' lines. No lymphadenopathy.

findings.pattern: Reduced amplitude, markedly slow velocity — demyelinating
Markedly slow velocity, prolonged DML, absent F-wave — CIDP pattern

findings.conduction_block: Present at fibular head — 42% amplitude reduction
findings.pattern: Conduction block — pathognomonic of demyelinating neuropathy/CIDP
Temporal dispersion + slow velocity — demyelinating, CIDP pattern

emg_findings.comment: Secondary axonal loss from chronic demyelination

quantitative_data.pattern: Demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy — bilateral, proximal and distal; conduction block present; temporal dispersion; uniformly slow velocities; prolonged F-waves; consistent with CIDP

specialized_test.impression: Demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy — markedly slow motor conduction velocities (22–30 m/s; <75% lower limit of normal), prolonged distal motor latencies, conduction block (>20% amplitude reduction right peroneal nerve at fibular head), temporal dispersion on median motor studies, absent F-waves. EMG demonstrates 1+ fibrillations and mild chronic neurogenic motor unit changes in tibialis anterior and proximal muscles bilaterally (vastus lateralis, deltoid) — consistent with secondary axonal loss superimposed on a demyelinating process. Findings meet established electrodiagnostic criteria for a demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy with both proximal and distal involvement. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Sural nerve biopsy shows evidence of demyelination and remyelination — onion bulb formations (lamellar Schwann cell proliferation) and perivascular mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates in the endoneurium and perineurium. No amyloid deposits, no vasculitis, no neoplastic infiltration. Findings are consistent with an inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: CIDP treatment IVIG vs plasmapheresis vs prednisone comparative

results.title: CIDP treatment guidelines — ICE trial and European CIDP study
results.key_finding: IVIG and plasmapheresis are equivalent first-line treatments; corticosteroids are effective but long-term steroid side effects limit use; IVIG preferred for acute treatment; newer subcutaneous IgG maintenance is available

results.title: CIDP remission — proportion who can stop treatment
results.key_finding: 30-40% of CIDP patients achieve sustained remission and can discontinue treatment; regular re-evaluation for treatment de-escalation is recommended

output.summary: Published guidelines and randomized controlled trials (including the ICE trial) support IVIG and plasmapheresis as equivalent first-line immunotherapy options for CIDP. Corticosteroids demonstrate efficacy but are associated with long-term side effects limiting sustained use. Subcutaneous immunoglobulin is an emerging maintenance option. Population-level data indicate 30–40% of patients achieve sustained remission allowing treatment de-escalation.

key_reasoning_points: CIDP is distinguished by: (1) proximal AND distal involvement; (2) demyelinating NCS (velocity <75% LLN, conduction block, temporal dispersion); (3) elevated CSF protein with normal cell count; (4) duration >8 weeks
The proximal lower and upper extremity involvement (hip girdle + shoulders) is the key feature distinguishing CIDP from length-dependent diabetic/toxic neuropathy
Conduction block (42% amplitude reduction at fibular head) is pathognomonic of an acquired demyelinating neuropathy
IVIG is first-line treatment with evidence for both acute improvement and maintenance

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Bilateral proximal-distal weakness with absent reflexes and demyelinating NCS is not deconditioning. CIDP requires prompt recognition and treatment.
